summary:
Bolívar department stands under Colombia's national framework. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, marriage equality has been available since 2016, and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Bolívar is itself the site of a documented trans killing. Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025; El Tiempo's data investigation calls the case a trans feminicide. More than 19 days later the circumstances remained unclear. Her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality.

The national toll is recorded at scale, and the official counts do not agree with each other or with civil society. The Fiscalía's own database records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, including 431 for 2024 against about 160 reported by the NGO, a discrepancy of 267. One Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data shows 39 homicides against 156 in the policies-and-strategies base. Experts cited in the investigation describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025. Violence escalates along a continuum from discrimination to intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims), then homicide and impunity. The report documents territorial expansion toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, together with insufficient state response. It does not name Bolívar explicitly; the department nevertheless sits within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for that expansion and weakest response, and the Carmen de Bolívar killing is covered by the El Tiempo investigation.
tangentialFactors:
Official and civil-society counts of LGBTIQ+ homicides diverge sharply in the same period, which affects how a visitor should read any single figure: 431 homicides for 2024 in the Fiscalía database against roughly 160 reported by the NGO, and 39 against 156 across two 2025 datasets within the same institution. The discrepancy is attributed by cited experts to an information system that is neither unified nor reliable.

Targeting elsewhere in Colombia follows an organised pattern. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, drowning in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was", President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Protection machinery exists nationally but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.

Bolívar does not appear by name in the Caribe Afirmativo report; its inclusion rests on the department's position within the flagged Caribbean-coast cluster and on the Carmen de Bolívar case documented separately by El Tiempo.
localsOnly:
Residents change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route open since the rule change approved in June 2015; judges no longer order bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments for that purpose. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Entry to public and commercial premises is protected by Constitutional Court judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk). A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict. A May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country.

Local trans advocacy continues through figures such as Yirley Velasco, who leads and remembers the work of Nawar Jiménez in Carmen de Bolívar, and through the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement of survivors of sexual violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
The circumstances of Nawar Jiménez's killing on 22 May 2025 in Carmen de Bolívar remained unresolved more than 19 days later, according to the El Tiempo investigation; no later finding is sourced here.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report does not name Bolívar. The department's placement within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for territorial expansion of violence and weakest state response is an inference from the report's regional framing combined with the Carmen de Bolívar case, not a department-level finding in the report itself.

No department-level homicide count for Bolívar is available in this inventory. The figures cited (3,322 since 2010, 431 for 2024, 39 and 156 for 2025) are national, and the sources describe the underlying information system as neither unified nor reliable.

The status of comprehensive trans legislation pending before the Colombian Congress is not resolved in this inventory; no enacted text or date is sourced here.

Whether the "trans" and "non-binary" markers introduced nationally in November 2025 are being issued without friction at notary and registry offices in Bolívar is not sourced in this inventory.
